name: libsixel
why: Renders real images as SIXEL graphics in terminals, a forgotten 1980s display protocol revived; a strong quick payoff.

brief.what_it_is: libsixel is an encoder and decoder library for DEC SIXEL graphics, a terminal-friendly image format, plus command-line converters. img2sixel takes image files (the README mentions JPEG, PNG and animated GIF, via libjpeg, libpng and related build options) from file arguments or stdin and writes a SIXEL escape-sequence stream to stdout or a named file. sixel2png goes the other way, turning a SIXEL file into a PNG. Because the output is plain escape sequences, you can cat it to a SIXEL-capable terminal to display the picture. The package also ships C APIs and bindings for Python, Perl, PHP and Ruby.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says SIXEL was built for 1980s DEC printers and terminals, where drawing images was painfully slow, and that modern CPUs and networks make the format practical again. It also says the author's encoder was redesigned for terminal emulators rather than dot-matrix printers, to reduce the transport overhead while staying compatible with older SIXEL terminals.
brief.how_it_works: SIXEL data is an escape sequence (DCS) stream, so any program that can write bytes to a terminal can show an image. The encoder quantizes colours (median-cut, with selectable dithering such as Floyd-Steinberg, Atkinson and Stucki) and emits the bands of six pixel rows that SIXEL uses, with an encoding policy aimed at terminal display speed rather than printer head movement. The decoder reverses this into an indexed bitmap plus palette.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is the package manager here, but the README lists many others (apt, pacman, nix, MacPorts and so on). Build from source uses ./configure, make and make install. Optional features are switched on or off with configure flags: --with-libcurl, --with-gd, --with-gdk-pixbuf2, --with-jpeg, --with-png, --enable-python, --enable-tests and others. Python bindings need either a configure --enable-python install or a manual build, and the README says the Python work is only on the develop branch. Perl, PHP and Ruby interfaces have their own build steps. A MinGW cross-build for Windows is documented. No accounts or runtime services are needed.
brief.standout: Rather than a printer-era encoder, it is a modern converter aimed at showing images in terminals: the README describes a terminal-oriented encoding that keeps compatibility with old DEC SIXEL terminals. The README also lists a wide set of real terminals and downstream projects (mlterm, WezTerm, iTerm2, xterm, RetroArch, Neofetch, and more), so the protocol is supported well beyond this one tool.
brief.status: unknown. The README shows a Travis CI badge and Coveralls badge, but gives no release date, version number or last-commit date, and the fetched page was truncated before any release or changelog information. The README points to a develop branch for the Python work. I did not check the GitHub releases or commit history, so I cannot give a firm status.
brief.caveats: By default img2sixel writes 7-bit output, and the README says terminals using an 8-bit mode need -8. Many terminals only support a 16-colour palette unless you configure them, and the README says xterm needs --enable-sixel-graphics at compile time and extra X resources set for more colours. Python bindings have a documented source-only path on develop. Some documented features (GIF animation, color quantization variants) are options, not defaults. The README support note says the software is provided as is and that the GitHub issue tracker is the main support channel. The README is cut off at 40000 characters, so the full licence text and any later sections were not seen. The licence is MIT per the README.
